notes.text: White opens by pushing the king's pawn two squares.
notes.original:
Watch a video of this lesson here:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kZJcQZoM7ZE

notes.text: Your pawn takes its own share of the centre and opens lines for your bishop and queen.
Your knight defends the e5 pawn that White's knight just attacked.
This bishop move starts the Ruy Lopez.
notes.original: These moves mark the start of the Ruy Lopez opening

notes.text: Your knight hits the e4 pawn at once, and you leave White's bishop on b5 alone.
notes.original: Ruy Lopez: Berlin Defense. Black leaves the bishop on b5 (rather than chasing it with a6) and immediately attacks the e4 pawn. In some lines, Black will play Nxe4 followed by a retreat Nd6, which will gain a tempo on the bishop on b5. We will look at four moves for White: 4.O-O, 4.d3, 4.Qe2 and 4.d4. The move 4.Nc3 leads to the Four Knights Game and will be studied in another lesson.

notes.text: White lets you take e4, planning Re1 to win the pawn back by pressuring e5.
notes.original: White allows the e4 pawn to be taken with the idea of playing Re1 and recovering his pawn by pressuring Black's e5 pawn.

notes.text: White protects e4 and plays slowly, planning c3 and d4 to build the center.
notes.original: Here, White simply protects e4 and plays the game more slowly. White may build up in the center with c3 and d4.

notes.text: White's queen protects the e4 pawn and puts pressure down the e-file.
notes.original: White protects e4 and puts pressure down the e-file.

notes.text: White strikes the center with d4, but the trades leave you with a comfortable, defensible position.
notes.original: Uncommon response. Inaccuracy. This attacks the center by offering a pawn and/or knight trade. However, this trades away too much material in the center, reducing white's initial tempo advantage by creating a more equal position that is defensible by black.

notes.text: White's knight guards e4 and the bishop, but blocks the c-pawn and lets you trade with Nd4.
notes.original: Four Knights Spanish Variation. White's 3rd most common response. This develops the queen's side knight, defending the e4 pawn and the light-squared bishop. This comes at a cost of obstructing the c-pawn, which prevents any c3 support for d4, and allows black to trade knights with tempo with Nd4. This variation will be covered in a future study by Coldfield1994.

notes.text: White gives up the bishop pair; retake with dxc6, and your knight also hits the loose e4 pawn.
notes.original: White's 4th most common response, seen more at low-level. Inaccuracy. This trades the light-squared bishop for the c6 knight, damaging black's pawn structure and removing the defender of the e5 pawn, allowing Nxe5. However, this loses the bishop pair and leaves the e4 pawn hanging to Nxe4. Additionally, by breaking principle and recapturing away from the center with dxc6, black opens up its queen and creates a strong defensive pawn structure on the queen's side, which black can later castle queen's side under.

notes.text: This is the Halloween attack, a dubious pawn grab that works worse than the Halloween gambit.
notes.original: 4.Nxe5?? is the so-called Halloween attack. It resembles the well-known Halloween gambit, but worse because Nc3 has been replaced by Bb5, reducing White's space advantage.

notes.text: Taking the pawn aims for an open position.
notes.original: We play for an open position.

notes.text: This bishop move is bad: White plays c3 and d4 anyway, gaining a tempo on your bishop.
notes.original: This is a bad move because White can respond with c3, which White likes to play anyway in Italian/Spanish positions to make a big center with d4. Thus, after c3 (immediately, or after Re1), White is simply a tempo up with respect to "normal" variants.

notes.text: This bishop move is the Beverwijk Variation of the Berlin Defense.
notes.original: This is called the Beverwijk Variation of the Berlin Defense.

notes.text: Your bishop shelters the king and prepares castling, so ...Nxe4 becomes a bigger threat.
notes.original: 4...Be7 before taking the pawn shelters Black's king and gets ready to castle. This prevents any mischief around a discovered check. Now the threat of 5...Nxe4 is more severe, as while White can still recover the pawn, they would have to give up the bishop pair to do so (e.g. 5.c3?! Nxe4 6.Re1 Nd6 7.Bxc6 dxc6 8.Nxe5 Bf5). 4...Be7 functionally declines the gambit, as it gives White time to play 5.Re1 and defend the e4 pawn. It is typically a quieter continuation.

notes.text: Your knight invites White to take it, but that would open the h-file against White's king.
notes.original:
4...Ng4?!, the Fishing pole variation, invites White to blunder by accepting a sacrificial knight but opening the h-file and exposing themselves to potential checkmate.

Black's knight forays into White's territory. This leads to a trap where Black baits White into opening the h-file.

White can sidestep the trap by leaving Black's knight on g4 and continuing to develop normally: 6.c3 intending d4, 6.d4, 6.Nc3 are all playable and leave White with the advantage.

The same trap can arise out of the Morphy defence, after 3...a6 4.Ba4 Nf6 5.O-O Ng4.

notes.text: This defends e5 and frees your bishop, but White answers d4, often pushing d5 for space.
notes.original: Improved Steinitz Defense. Black's 2nd most common response, seen more at low-level. Mistake. This solidly defends the e5 pawn, opening up the light-squared bishop which could potentially pin white's f3 knight to its queen with Bg4. This essentially transposes to a slightly better-for-black version of the Steinitz Defense where white has castled king's side instead of having played d4. However, this allows white to counterattack the center with d4, often playing d5 to gain a space advantage or damaging black's pawn structure after a pawn, knight, and bishop trade. This variation will be covered in a future study by Coldfield1994.

notes.text: White welcomes a trade on d4, because it drags your e-pawn off its file and exposes your king.
notes.original: Uncommon response. Slight blunder. This centralizes the c6 knight, offering a knight trade or forcing the light-squared bishop to move and risk black trading knights anyway. However, white wants to trade knights as this moves the e5 pawn off of the e-file, opening up black's king more, allowing e5, and overextending black's pawn.

notes.text: Asking the bishop with a6 is a slight blunder: Bxc6 and Nxe5 win your e5 pawn.
notes.original: Uncommon response. Slight blunder. This attempts to push away the light-squared bishop similarly to the Morphy Defense. However, this wastes a tempo, lets white damage black's pawn structure, and loses a pawn as white can sacrifice the bishop pair with Bxc6 and then win the e5 pawn with Nxe5. Black can't capture the e4 pawn in retaliation with Nxe4, as white can pin the e4 knight to the king with Re1.

notes.text: Bd6 is a blunder: after d4, taking on d4 allows e5, forking your bishop and knight.
notes.original: Uncommon response. Blunder. This develops the dark-squared bishop, adding another defender to the e5 pawn and bringing black closer to castling king's side. However, this allows white to tactically attack the center with d4. Black can't capture with exd4 or Nxd4 without hanging a pawn fork with e5. Additionally, this threatens to capture the e5 pawn with dxe5 after Bxc6, leading to a pawn fork, so black must defend e5 again or move its dark-squared bishop.

notes.text: White gambits a pawn, hoping the open lines will help an attack on your king.
notes.original: The main line and an attempt at an improvement over the immediate 5.Re1. White gambits a pawn in hopes of opening up lines to the Black king.

notes.text: This leads to a quieter game; White will win back the pawn by taking on e5.
notes.original: This will result in a quieter game than 5.d4. White will recover their pawn by taking on e5.

notes.text: White regains the pawn another way; you carry on in the same way, with the knight to d6.
notes.original: Instead of 5.Re1, this is another way to regain the pawn. We should proceed similarly.

notes.text: White gives up the bishop pair; retake with dxc6 to open your queen and light-squared bishop.
notes.original: Uncommon response, seen more at low-level. Mistake. This trades the light-squared bishop for the c6 knight, removing the defender of the e5 pawn and allowing Nxe5. However, this loses the bishop pair and allows black to open up its queen and light-squared bishop after dxc6, which is strictly weaker than winning the e5 pawn with Re1 or attacking the center with d4.

notes.text: Taking on d4 was too dangerous; your knight retreats with a tempo on the bishop.
notes.original: It was too dangerous to take the gambit pawn on d4. Our knight has now gained a tempo on the b5-bishop. We will consider two responses.

notes.text: Your pawn kicks the bishop, so you can prepare ...d5 without the pin on your knight.
notes.original:
Alternatively, if Black could play ...d5, they could support their knight in the centre and perhaps keep the e-file closed for now. However, 5...d5? in this position pins Black's knight and allows 6.Nxe5!. Black must prepare it with 5...a6, the Rosenthal Variation, where 6.Ba4 transposes into an Open Spanish and Black gets to play ...d5: 6...b5 7.Bb3 d5.

Black now kicks White's bishop. Removing its pressure from Black's knight will allow Black to play ...d5, expanding in the centre and defending the knight on e4, without dropping a pawn due to the pin.

Any retreat along the f1-a6 diagonal the bishop travelled on move 3 constitutes a loss of tempo and allows ...d5. The two serious possibilities are 6.Bxc6 or 6.Ba4.

notes.text: Your bishop shelters the king and prepares castling, which makes the open centre less dangerous.
notes.original: 5...Be7, the Rio de Janeiro variation, shelters the king and prepares to castle, after which an open centre is less dangerous. The game continues 6.Qe2 Nd6 7.Bxc6 bxc6! 8.dxe5 Nb7 9.Nc3 O-O. This was how this position was played in the 19th century.

notes.text: Taking on d4 is a mistake: White plays Re1 and pins your e4 knight to your king.
notes.original: Black's 2nd most common response, seen more at low-level. Mistake. This trades the d4 pawn, trying to trade knights and leave white's light-squared bishop aiming at nothing. However, this allows white to pin the e4 knight to black's king with Re1, forcing black to damage its pawn structure to defend the knight.

notes.text: Defending the knight with d5 is a blunder: White wins the e5 pawn with a tactic.
notes.original: Uncommon response. Blunder. This attempts to defend the e4 knight. However, this allows black to tactically capture the e5 pawn with Nxe5, leading to either a Nxf7 sacrifice to win a few pawns, the e4 knight, and black's castling rights, or trading with the c6 knight and forking the king and rook with Bxc6.

notes.text: Capturing on d4 is a blunder: White pins your e4 knight to the king and wins it.
notes.original: Uncommon response. Blunder. This attempts to trade knights and pawns by capturing the d4 pawn. However, this allows white to pin the e4 knight to the black king after the trades, forcing black to defend with f5 and losing the knight to f3.

notes.text: This is the main line: you retake and the queens will soon be traded.
notes.original: The main line, leading to a trade of queens.

notes.text: This rare capture seems to lose a piece for White, but it doesn't.
notes.original: This rare move seems to lose a piece, but it doesn't.

notes.text: After the retreat you can take on d4 or push e4; either way it is equal.
notes.original: White could retreat the bishop, 6.Ba4 the Showalter variation, which allows Black to take the pawn 6...exd4 or push 6...e4 to where their pawn is defended by the knight. The game is thought equal either way.

notes.text: White's bishop attacks your queen; block with Be7 or f6.
notes.original: Uncommon response. This develops the dark-squared bishop, attacking black's queen and forcing black to obstruct, usually with Be7 or f6, forcing the dark-squared bishop to move again or trade with one of black's minor pieces.

notes.text: Your c-pawns are doubled, but your bishop and queen get open lines and the d-file is half-open.
notes.original: Black's strongest, most common response. This breaks an opening principle by recapturing white's light-squared bishop away from the center. Because of this, black both opens up its light-squared bishop and creates a semi-open d-file. This allows white a tactical response that trades queens and wins black's castling rights, but black argues that it has a strong defensive position even with the damaged pawns and lack of castling rights and can force a draw from that position.

notes.text: Recapturing with the b-pawn leaves doubled c-pawns and an isolated a-pawn that White can target.
notes.original: Black's 2nd most common response, seen more at low-level. Slight blunder. This recaptures white's light-squared bishop by following normal opening principles by capturing towards the center. However, this allows white to either trade dark-squared bishops or damage the king's side pawn structure with Bg5. Without either the bishop pair or a strong defensive position for the king, white can take advantage of black's three pawn islands and usually can win at least an additional pawn.

notes.text: White's e5 pawn hits your knight; if it moves, White's queen faces your queen on the d-file.
notes.original: White's strongest, most common response. This captures black's hanging e5 pawn, putting pressure on the d6 knight, forcing it to move which will expose black's queen to a discovery attack by white's queen.

notes.text: White's knight grabs e5 but is overextended, giving you time to play Be7 and castle.
notes.original: White's 2nd most common response. Mistake. This captures the hanging e5 pawn while centralizing white's knight. This also puts some pressure on the f7 pawn, leading to potential threats to black's king. However, this gives black critical tempo to safely castle king's side, starting with Be7. Additionally, the e5 knight is slightly overextended, a target for black to pressure, giving black a slight advantage.

notes.text: Re1 pins your e5 pawn, but you save it with e4, which also hits the f3 knight.
notes.original: Uncommon response. Slight blunder. This brings the rook to the semi-open e-file, pinning black's e5 pawn to its king. However, this gives black critical tempo to save its e5 pawn by advancing it with e4. On e4 the pawn both is defended and pressures the f3 knight, potentially threatening to capture it when the pawn becomes unpinned.

notes.text: The f5 square is stable for your knight; it can later go to g6 or h4.
notes.original: The most stable square for the knight. From f5, it may also go to e7 and then to g6 in some lines. Or it may go to h4 after a preparatory Be7.

notes.text: This is the l'Hermet Variation, also called the Westerinen Variation.
notes.original: l'Hermet Variation - Westerinen Variation

notes.text: Nc4 is an uncommon way to move your attacked knight.
notes.original: (1.72@56) Uncommon response.

notes.text: Nb5 is an uncommon way to move your attacked knight.
notes.original: Uncommon response.

notes.text: The Berlin Wall: tuck your king on e8, develop your bishops, bring a rook to d8, and maybe play Nh4.
notes.original: The Berlin Wall Defense. Our plan will be: Ke8, Be7, Be6, Rd8, and possibly Nh4 to either trade with the f3-knight or fall back to g6. We can activate the h8-rook by pushing our h-pawn. Our king should be safe on e8. We will explore a couple of sample lines.

notes.text: A very popular, flexible developing move for White.
notes.original: A very popular flexible move.

notes.text: White develops the rook with check, so your king has to move.
notes.original: The appeal of this move is to develop the rook with tempo, giving check to the black king

notes.text: White shows its kingside pawn majority and plans to advance those pawns later.
notes.original: This is immediately signifying white's pawn majority and their planning to advance the kingside pawns in the future.

notes.text: Your king leaves the open d-file before White's rook can check it there.
This move keeps pieces off g4, though none were heading there; it may simply be a waiting move.
notes.original: I'm not sure why this move is so popular. It does keep a pieces off the g4 square, and perhaps White intends to play g4, but no pieces were yet threatening to come to g4. Perhaps it is another flexible move and White is waiting to see what Black will do.

notes.text: Your knight must clear the light bishop's path, so it is heading for h4.
notes.original: We'd like to get the f5-knight out of the way of our light-squared bishop. So, it's heading for h4.

notes.text: Your h-pawn slows White's kingside pawn advance by controlling the g4 square.
notes.original: Black plays this move in order to slow white down on the kingside.

notes.text: Your knight offers a trade on f3 and clears the diagonal for your light bishop.
You take the knight back and keep both bishops against White's bishop and knight.
Your light bishop finally comes out and eyes White's c2 pawn.
Your king steps out of check without blocking your dark bishop, as e7 would.
Your bishop develops and covers d8 and g5, the squares White's pieces want.
Your knight heads for g6, where it is more useful than on f5.
notes.original: Black plans to put his knight on g6 so that it can be useful rather than staying on f5.

notes.text: The position may well be a draw.
notes.original: Draw...?

notes.text: You swap off White's active bishop, leaving it with only knights against your bishop.
Your pawn attacks the undefended knight on g5, so it must retreat.
Your bishop develops and covers d5 and d7, keeping White's knight and rook out.
Your knight took the bishop, but White's a-pawn push leaves it short of safe squares.
notes.original: Altough the Knight is took the Bishop after a4 it has nowhere to go.

notes.text: The a-pawn traps your knight on b5, so you will have to give a piece back.
notes.original: Our knight is trapped, and we will have to give back a piece.

notes.text: Your trapped knight escapes to d4, where your other knight backs it up for a trade.
You take back the knight; White's queen will capture yours, but you keep both bishops.
The position is about equal: you have the bishop pair and only need to catch up in development.
notes.original: The position is about equal. We have the bishop pair, and just need to catch up a little in development.

notes.text: Your knight retreats and attacks the bishop on b5.
notes.original: Attacking the bishop on b5.

notes.text: White regains the pawn, and the knight on e5 now shields a discovered check from the rook.
notes.original: White recovers the pawn and threatens discovered checks on the e-file. Here, 6...Be7 is the favored move, but the move we will choose is more forcing and will likely transpose to the main move anyway.

notes.text: White gives up the bishop pair, which makes White's development easier.
notes.original: This move just gives up the bishop pair and makes our development easier.

notes.text: Take the knight before it can move away and uncover a rook check.
You have equalized: the pawns are symmetrical, and White's rook and bishop can be chased away.
notes.original: Black managed to equalize the position, the pawns are symmetrical and the developed white rook and bishop can be chased away

notes.text: The usual retreat: the bishop steps out of the way of White's other pieces.
notes.original: The usual retreat. The bishop is out of the way of the other pieces.

notes.text: Castling releases the pin on your bishop, because your king leaves the e-file.
notes.original: Releasing the pin on our bishop.

notes.text: White's centre pawn gives a simple, healthy position that many new players are happy to reach.
notes.original:
Already reaching this position will be a great start for many new players.
If you want to go more in depth, I have added deeper analysis as well

notes.text: Your bishop hits the rook on e5, and once it leaves, your knight can jump to f5.
notes.original: We want to drive the rook back and gain the f5-square for our knight.

notes.text: White can also put the rook on e2, where it is sometimes more useful.
notes.original:
Is another option, claiming that it sometimes can be more useful to have
the rook on e2. I won't cover it in detail here though

notes.text: Your knight and bishop both hit d4 and your d-pawn is free; White is only slightly better.
notes.original: This releases our d-pawn to be pushed forward and attacks the d4-pawn. The position looks about equal, but our pieces are more awkwardly placed, so White may have a nagging slight advantage.

notes.text: Your rook offers a trade on the e-file; offering trades is a usual Black strategy in the Berlin.
notes.original:
Black goes
for a trade of rooks. Offering trades is a usual strategy for black in the
Berlin

notes.text: White's c-pawn now protects the d4 pawn.
notes.original: White protects d4.

notes.text: White grabs space with the d5 pawn, but that opens the diagonal for your f6 bishop.
notes.original:
Is
perhaps a more ambitious try, aiming to claim space because of the d5-pawn.
There are also some downsides as well, one being the opening of the black
bishop on f6, and also having a slightly more problematic development

notes.text: You take your share of the center; next bring your knight to d6 and your bishop to f5.
notes.original: We get our share of the center. Now, our plan is to move our knight to d6 and then our bishop to f5.

notes.text: Taking back with the d-pawn frees your light bishop and keeps both bishops.
Your bishop shields the king on the open e-file and clears the way to castle.
Unlike the main line, your knight doesn't block the d-pawn and your light bishop is already free.
notes.original: Compare this to the main line. Here, our knight on d6 is not blocking a d-pawn, and our light-squared bishop is already free to move.

notes.text: Your knight attacks the bishop on b5.
notes.original: Attacking the bishop.

notes.text: Recapturing with the d-pawn opens your light bishop's diagonal and leaves you both bishops.
White's queen checks and eyes g7, so blocking with the bishop on e7 would drop that pawn.
notes.original: Now we can't play 7...Be7, dropping the g7 pawn, and we prefer not to play 7...Be6 and face 8.Nd4. So:

notes.text: Your queen blocks the check and offers a trade, while your bishop stays guarding g7.
Your queen clears e7 for the bishop, but White can repeat with a queen check on e5.
notes.original: We vacate the e7 square for our bishop. However, White can repeat with 9.Qe5+. If we don't want a draw, we'll have to try blocking the queen check with 9...Be6.

notes.text: Your bishop gets a nice diagonal, pointing at f2.
notes.original: We get our bishop out to a nice diagonal.

notes.text: The Mortimer move gambits e5: if White takes it, c6 and ...Qa5+ fork the knight.
notes.original:
4...Ne7, the Mortimer variation, is a sideline. This gambits the e5 pawn, but if White takes it, they fall into the devious Mortimer trap: 5.Nxe5 c6 6.Bc4 Qa5+!, forking the knight with check.

4...Ne7 in the Anti-Berlin is the Mortimer variation. On the surface this is a strange move: Black violates principles by moving their knight a second time in the opening, at the same time inhibiting the development of their king-side bishop. Black's idea is to free the c6 square for their pawn, and chase White's bishop away that way.

Therefore 5.O-O is the mainline, removing the king from the centre and any ideas of Qa5+. After 5...c6 6.Ba4 Black must defend e5, either with 6...d6 or by moving the knight again, 6...Ng6.

The Mortimer variation is named after James Mortimer (1832―1911), who played it at a tournament in London in 1883.

notes.text: a6 is a mistake: White takes your knight and then wins a pawn.
notes.original: This is mistake. White can get a pawn by taking the knight.

notes.text: White starts building the center, but you strike first with ...d5.
notes.original: Starting to build up the center. But we will beat him to it.

notes.text: You open the game for quick development, and you now threaten to take the e4 pawn.
notes.original: The usual move was 5...O-O, but we prefer to open up the game and get quick development. We are threatening to take the e4-pawn. We will consider three responses.

notes.text: Now that you've castled, White plans Bg5 to pin your knight on f6.
notes.original: If opponent castled, pin the knight.

notes.text: After your d6, White can play d4 right away.
notes.original: If this, you can play d4 immediately.

notes.text: White's knight now attacks your e5 pawn.
notes.original: Now our e-pawn is under attack.

notes.text: White's knight protects e4 and shields the queen from a possible queen trade.
notes.original: White protects e4 and shields his queen from a possible queen-trade.

notes.text: White's d4 pawn hits both your e5 pawn and your bishop, so you have to take it.
notes.original: Attacking both our pawn and our bishop. Our hand is forced.

notes.text: Your queen takes on d5 and protects the e5 pawn.
notes.original: We defend e5.

notes.text: White's bishop attacks your queen, with the f7 square behind it.
notes.original: Attacking the queen and the f7 square behind it.

notes.text: Your queen is well placed on d6: it guards e5 and clears the bishop's path. White has a slight edge.
notes.original: The queen is well placed on d6. It protects e5, it is out of the way of our light-squared bishop, and the move Bg5 will not pin our knight. The game is open and tactical, and White probably has just a slight edge.

notes.text: Your pawn takes on e4 and threatens the knight on f3, so White must take back.
Think about what happens if White takes your knight on c6 and then your e5 pawn.
notes.original: We have to consider what happens if White takes our c6-knight and then our e5-pawn.

notes.text: If White goes after your e5 pawn, you can answer with Re8 or Qe7.
notes.original: If White tries to win the e5-pawn, we are ready to play Re8 or Qe7.

notes.text: Taking the pawn ends the attack on your bishop, which now guards your pawn on d4.
Your attacked knight jumps to the centre, where it hits the f2 and c3 pawns.
You have reached a known Italian Game line, the Center Attack, by transposition.
notes.original: We have transposed to a line in the Italian Game: Center Attack!

notes.text: White gave up the bishop pair, and your light-squared bishop now has an open diagonal.
notes.original: I think White has just handed over the bishop-pair and opened a diagonal for our light-squared bishop. Note that he cannot win a pawn with 6.Nxe5 because of the response 6...Qd4. There are many moves White can consider here, and White will soon be threatening our e5 pawn. Our plan to protect e5 in most cases is to play solidly with Nd7, O-O, and f6. Then to complete development, we may play Re8 and Nf8 to release our light-squared bishop. Let's look at one example line.

notes.text: White's castling makes taking on e5 a threat, so protect that pawn.
notes.original: This makes Nxe5 a threat.

notes.text: Your knight steps back to guard the e5 pawn that White was ready to take.
Your king gets safe, and your rook can now slide to e8 behind the e5 pawn.
White's second knight joins the attack on your e5 pawn.
notes.original: Attacking e5 again.

notes.text: Your rook backs up the e5 pawn, so two defenders now meet White's two knights.
The f6 pawn frees your knight to travel to f8.
notes.original: This move releases our knight to move to f8.

notes.text: You were planning this knight jump to d4 all along, once White allowed it.
notes.original: We were planning on making this move if allowed.

notes.text: You win the knight back, and your bishop lands in the centre hitting b2 and f2.
Your bishop steps away from the c3 pawn but stays on the diagonal aimed at f2.
This bishop pins your f6 knight; you plan to break the pin with h6.
notes.original: Not a popular move, but we confess that we fear getting our f6-knight pinned like this. Our plan is to break the pin with h6 and g5.

notes.text: Your pawn hits the pinning bishop, so it must trade itself off or step back.
Play c6 before g5, so that after the bishop reaches g3 you can protect e5 with d6.
notes.original: It is important to insert this move before g5 because after White's bishop goes to g3, we want to be able to protect e5 with the move d6.

notes.text: Your pawn chases the bishop away and frees your knight from the pin for good.
The engine says you have an advantage here, and you like the position.
notes.original: The engine actually says we have an advantage in this position! We do like it.

notes.text: Your bishop is active and you threaten to simplify with your knight to d4.
notes.original: We develop our bishop to an active diagonal and get ready to castle. If White wins our e-pawn, we will quickly get a rook to e8. Also, with our bishop on c5, we are threatening to simplify with Nd4.

notes.text: White's c3 pawn takes the d4 square away from your knight.
notes.original: White prevents Nd4.

notes.text: Your king gets safe first, so you can then strike in the centre with d5.
You control d4, so White pushes d3 modestly to free the dark-squared bishop.
notes.original: Note that Black has the d4-square under control. So, White modestly pushes the pawn to d3 to get the dark-squared bishop out.

notes.text: You open the position with d5, hitting the e4 pawn; White has four replies to consider.
